title: Kamar: iron, household work and village tools
description: Kamar histories in Odisha through household iron smelting, women’s work, practical learning and village tool-making and repair.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
lead: Who supplied the iron tools on which village work depended? Kamar histories bring together craft, household labour and relationships with cultivators. Regional records reveal different arrangements, rather than one occupation practised in exactly the same way everywhere.

paragraphs.text: The Ganjam District Gazetteer places Kamar within a broader description of Biswakarma communities, alongside Badhei and Pathuria. It distinguishes their work with iron, wood and stone respectively, and records Biswakarma worship. Iron implements and household appliances are the Kamar products named in this account.

This regional grouping connects crafts without making the names interchangeable. It does not establish the identity of everyone who works iron or worships Biswakarma. Nor does a list of useful products explain when a community first formed.
paragraphs.locator: Interpretation and limits of regional account

paragraphs.text: A 1962 study of Penthabahal’s Kamar smelters describes women gathering ore, carrying charcoal and operating paired foot bellows. A clay furnace supplied hot iron for working on a granite anvil. The report describes learning by watching elders. Production required several people’s labour.

The Daanla village study, investigated in 1962 and published in 1968, records one Kamar household. Separately, it describes the village blacksmith making axes, sickles, ploughshares and knives, and repairing agricultural implements. Households with draught animals paid six seers of paddy annually for each pair of bullocks. The payment followed the agricultural household’s animals, rather than a price charged for every repaired tool.
paragraphs.locator: Printed7,38; household record and service account remain distinct

paragraphs.text: Cultivators made wooden handles themselves, while metal parts came from the market or the local smith. Surplus smith-made goods were sold in neighbouring villages or Keonjhar market. These details show work shared between makers and users, with a market beyond the village. They describe Daanla at the time of the study, not a statewide payment rule or a way to identify someone’s caste.

The crafts survey found smelting furnaces operating around Umarkot in 1961 but closed in several villages by late 1962. Smelters blamed restrictions on collecting ore from reserved forests. The author also discussed charcoal shortages and competition from factory iron. These are historical observations and attributed explanations, not a claim about conditions today.
paragraphs.locator: Printed15–16,49; testimony distinguished from verified legal finding

paragraphs.text: The evidence explains particular livelihoods and pressures on them. It supplies no verified founder or creation date for the Kamar community. Family histories and local accounts remain necessary to trace settlement and change; neither a surname nor metalworking alone identifies a person’s community.
